report:
Conclusion
- The evidence supports a meaningful difference: Model B (B minus A > 0) has stronger residual-stream signals that push toward vocabulary from the commercial/professional / local-business / culinary topic cluster (words like "professional", "Professional", "restaurant", "Restaurant", "cooking", "Cooking", "baking", "Chef", "Kitchen", "dissertation", "metropolitan", "Innovation", "billionaire", etc.).
- I would summarize the change as a topical prior shift toward professional / local‑business / restaurant & culinary content (and related technical/business words), not a change in low‑level decoding artifacts or a clear change in sentiment/safety.

Why I believe this
- The L2-norm of the difference is concentrated at higher layers (large spikes from about layer 10 up to 25), which is where the model encodes higher‑level semantics and topic priors rather than low‑level tokenization effects.
- The logit‑lens top tokens for the highest‑norm cells repeatedly contain the same semantic group: restaurant/cooking vocabulary (restaurant, cooking, Chef, baking, Kitchen, Cook), professional/resume/academic vocabulary (professional, Professional, dissertation, metropolitan, undergraduate, honors), plus business/technical words (billionaire, macroeconomic, polyurethane, petrochemical, Innovation). That repeated thematic pattern across many layers/positions is consistent with a change in topical activation rather than random noise.
- No strong, consistent signals point to a different objective class (e.g., toxicity, politeness, instruction following). The tokens are mostly topical.

Uncertainties / caveats
- The signal is a mixture (culinary/restaurant + professional/academic + some technical/business terms). That could reflect a narrower domain (e.g., "local business listings / restaurant reviews / bios") or a broader commercial/professional domain. The evidence does not single out one narrow subdomain more precisely than that.
- Patchscope continuations were not shown, so I rely on the logit‑lens tokens and layer norms; those give a strong topical signal but not behavioral readouts.

If you want, I can:
- Label which model (A vs B) corresponds to the topical increase if you confirm which sign (B−A) should be read as an increase for B,
- Run targeted patchscope injections or prompts (e.g., short identity prompts, bios, restaurant reviews) to verify the behavioral effect.
